---
title: "Quiz: splines on images"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

---

**Q1.** Nearest-neighbour and bilinear interpolation are B-splines of which degrees? What is the main fault of each?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Box and hat.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Degree 0 (box) and degree 1 (hat, in $x$ and in $y$). Nearest: blocky jumps, aliasing. Bilinear: kinks along pixel rows and columns (the slope jumps) and blur between pixels.
:::

---

**Q2.** Why can the pixel values not be used directly as the coefficients of a cubic B-spline interpolant?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Values of β³ at the integers.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The cubic B-spline is $\tfrac16, \tfrac46, \tfrac16$ at a pixel and its neighbours, so the resulting surface at a pixel is $\tfrac16(f_{k-1} + 4f_k + f_{k+1})$, a blurred value, not $f_k$. The coefficients must first be computed by the prefilter (solving $\tfrac16(c_{k-1} + 4c_k + c_{k+1}) = f_k$), which sharpens.
:::

---

**Q3.** Cubic convolution and the cubic B-spline (with prefilter) both use 4 × 4 pixels per output value. What is the difference?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Which values are weighted: pixels or coefficients?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Cubic convolution weights the **pixel values** with a fixed interpolating kernel (C¹, no preprocessing, strictly local). The B-spline weights **coefficients** obtained by the prefilter over whole rows and columns; the result is C² and closer to an ideal low-pass, at the cost of the prefilter pass.
:::

---

**Q4.** You rotate an image 10 times by 36°. Rank nearest, bilinear and cubic B-spline by how much the image changes, and explain the worst one.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Each rotation resamples the previous result.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Cubic B-spline (least: RMS 11.3 on the micrograph), bilinear (21.6), nearest (28.1). Nearest copies values from slightly wrong places each time; the position errors accumulate and edges become jagged. Bilinear blurs a little at every step and the blur accumulates.
:::

---

**Q5.** Why must a label image (object numbers) be warped with nearest neighbour even if the grey image is warped with a cubic B-spline?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What is the average of label 1 and label 3?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Any interpolator that weights several pixels invents values between labels (label 2 between 1 and 3, fractions near every boundary), and cubics even overshoot to values beyond the range. Labels are names, not quantities; nearest neighbour copies an existing label.
:::

---

**Q6.** In a free-form deformation with control spacing $h = 32$ pixels, one control point is dragged 12 pixels to the right. How far do the pixel at that control point and the pixel at the next control point move?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
$\beta^3(0)^2 = \tfrac49$, $\beta^3(1)\beta^3(0) = \tfrac19$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$12 \cdot \tfrac49 = 5.33$ pixels and $12 \cdot \tfrac19 = 1.33$ pixels (diagonally $12 \cdot \tfrac1{36} = 0.33$).
:::

---

**Q7.** What does a negative Jacobian determinant of a deformation mean, and how do you avoid it?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Local change of area, with a sign.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The map **folds**: a small region is mirrored, so parts of the image land on top of other parts and the map is not one-to-one. Keep control displacements small relative to the spacing (below about 0.49 of the spacing in 2D guarantees no folding), or penalise bending during registration.
:::

---

**Q8.** *(math)* Show that the frequency response of $\tfrac16[1\;4\;1]$ is $(2 + \cos\omega)/3$ and explain why the prefilter (its inverse) exists.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Apply the filter to $e^{i\omega k}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$\tfrac16(e^{-i\omega} + 4 + e^{i\omega}) = \tfrac16(4 + 2\cos\omega) = \tfrac{2 + \cos\omega}{3}$. It is at least $\tfrac13$ (at $\omega = \pi$) and never zero, so the inverse filter $3/(2 + \cos\omega)$ exists and amplifies by at most 3.
:::
